summary.text: Since the product is not $1$, the associated-prime set is nonempty, so it has a maximum $m$, which is prime and satisfies $m\le n$. If $2n-m$ were composite, it would have a prime divisor $q\le\sqrt{2n-m}\le\sqrt{2n}$; then $q\mid 2n-m$ would give $m\equiv2n\pmod q$, contradicting the defining modular avoidance condition, so $2n-m$ is prime and the resulting partition yields the global conclusion.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
M=2n,
\qquad r=\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor.
\]
For positive \(M\), define \(GB(M)\) to be the finite set of natural numbers \(p\) satisfying all of the following conditions:

1. \(p\) is prime;
2. \(r<p\);
3. \(p\le \lfloor M/2\rfloor\);
4. for every prime \(q\le r\),
   \[
   p\not\equiv M\pmod q.
   \]

For \(M=0\), set \(GB(0)=\varnothing\). The set is finite because it is contained in \(\{0,1,\ldots,\lfloor M/2\rfloor\}\).

This is the residue form of the Goldbach-associated condition in the sequence description. Indeed, if \(p\in GB(M)\) and \(q\le r\) is prime, then \(q<p\). Since \(p\) is prime, \(q\nmid p\). Consequently, the assertion that \(q\) does not divide the integer product \(p(p-M)\) is equivalent to \(q\nmid(p-M)\), which in turn is equivalent to \(p\not\equiv M\pmod q\).

The sequence is
\[
a(n)=\prod_{p\in GB(2n)}p,
\]
with the usual convention that the product over the empty set is \(1\). This formula also agrees with the special definition at \(n=0\), since then \(GB(0)=\varnothing\).

We will prove the following local assertion. If \(n\ge3\) and \(a(n)\ne1\), then \(GB(2n)\) is nonempty. Hence its maximum
\[
m=\max GB(2n)
\]
exists, and \(m\in GB(2n)\), every \(k\in GB(2n)\) satisfies \(k\le m\), and \(2n-m\) is prime. Since membership also says that \(m\) is prime, this makes \((2n-m,m)\) a Goldbach partition of \(2n\). We then derive the global implication to Goldbach’s conjecture.

We first record an elementary primality criterion.

**Primality criterion.** Suppose \(N\ge2\), and suppose that no prime \(q\le\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\) divides \(N\). Then \(N\) is prime.

To justify this, suppose instead that \(N\) were composite. Then \(N=de\) for integers \(d,e\) with \(2\le d<N\) and \(2\le e<N\). Interchanging the factors if necessary, we may assume \(d\le e\), so \(d^2\le de=N\), and hence \(d\le\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\). The integer \(d\ge2\) has a prime divisor \(q\). Then
\[
q\le d\le\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor
\]
and \(q\mid d\mid N\), contradicting the hypothesis. Thus \(N\) is prime.

We now prove the local assertion. Fix \(n\ge3\), assume \(a(n)\ne1\), and put
\[
M=2n,
\qquad G=GB(M).
\]
Since \(n\ge3\), we have \(M>0\), so the positive-\(M\) description of \(GB(M)\) applies.

First, \(G\) is nonempty. For if \(G=\varnothing\), then by the empty-product convention,
\[
a(n)=\prod_{p\in G}p=1,
\]
contrary to the assumption \(a(n)\ne1\).

Because \(G\) is a nonempty finite set of natural numbers, it has a maximum. Let
\[
m=\max G.
\]
By the defining property of a maximum,
\[
m\in G
\quad\text{and}\quad
k\le m\quad\text{for every }k\in G.
\]
Membership \(m\in G\) gives the following facts:
\[
m\text{ is prime},
\qquad
\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor<m,

yad
m\le \left\lfloor\frac M2\right\rfloor=n,
\]
and, for every prime \(q\le\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\),
\[
m\not\equiv M\pmod q. \tag{1}
\]
(The displayed “yad” is to be read as “and”; thus the third displayed condition is \(m\le\lfloor M/2\rfloor=n\).)

We claim that the complementary summand
\[
C=M-m=2n-m
\]
is prime. First, it is at least \(2\). Indeed, \(m\le n\), and therefore
\[
C=2n-m\ge2n-n=n\ge3.
\]
Thus \(C\ge2\).

It remains, by the primality criterion, to show that no prime at most \(\lfloor\sqrt C\rfloor\) divides \(C\). Let \(q\) be prime and suppose
\[
q\le\lfloor\sqrt C\rfloor.
\]
We first check that \(q\) belongs to the range of small primes tested in the definition of \(GB(M)\). Since \(m\ge0\),
\[
C=M-m\le M.
\]
Taking integer square roots gives
\[
\lfloor\sqrt C\rfloor\le\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor,
\]
so
\[
q\le\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, this square-root comparison can also be seen directly. If \(r=\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\), then
\[
M<(r+1)^2.
\]
As \(C\le M\), we have \(C<(r+1)^2\), which forces \(\lfloor\sqrt C\rfloor<r+1\), hence \(\lfloor\sqrt C\rfloor\le r\).

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(q\mid C=M-m\). Since \(m\le M\), there is no ambiguity in this natural-number difference, and
\[
M=(M-m)+m=C+m.
\]
Reducing this equality modulo \(q\), the divisibility \(q\mid C\) gives
\[
M\equiv m\pmod q. \tag{3}
\]
But \(q\) is prime and (2) says \(q\le\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\). Therefore the residue-avoidance property (1) of \(m\in GB(M)\) says precisely that
\[
m\not\equiv M\pmod q,
\]
contradicting (3). Hence \(q\nmid C\).

We have proved that every prime \(q\le\lfloor\sqrt C\rfloor\) fails to divide \(C\). Since \(C\ge2\), the primality criterion now yields that \(C=M-m=2n-m\) is prime.

This establishes every part of the local claim:

* \(GB(2n)\) is nonempty;
* \(m=\max GB(2n)\) belongs to \(GB(2n)\);
* every \(k\in GB(2n)\) satisfies \(k\le m\);
* \(2n-m\) is prime.

Moreover, because \(m\in GB(2n)\), \(m\) itself is prime. Also, from \(m\le n\le2n\),
\[
(2n-m)+m=2n.
\]
Thus
\[
(2n-m,m)
\]
is a pair of primes whose sum is \(2n\), i.e. a Goldbach partition of \(2n\). Notice that the primality argument actually proves a slightly stronger fact: every member \(p\in GB(2n)\) has prime complement \(2n-p\). Choosing the maximum is needed only to obtain the particular canonical element asserted in the conjecture.

Finally, assume the global hypothesis
\[
\forall k\ge3,
\qquad a(k)\ne1.
\]
Let \(n\ge3\) be arbitrary. Applying the local result to this \(n\), let \(m=\max GB(2n)\). Then both \(m\) and \(2n-m\) are prime, and
\[
2n=m+(2n-m).
\]
Therefore every even integer of the form \(2n\) with \(n\ge3\), equivalently every even integer at least \(6\), is the sum of two primes. This is exactly the stated form of Goldbach’s conjecture. Hence the condition \(a(n)\ne1\) for every \(n\ge3\) implies Goldbach’s conjecture, and the asserted local construction by \(m=\max GB(2n)\) holds whenever \(n\ge3\) and \(a(n)\ne1\).
